variants.question: Which state of matter is best described as one that has a definite shape and a definite volume?
Which state of matter is best described as one that has a definite volume but takes the shape of its container?
Which state of matter is best described as one that has neither a definite shape nor a definite volume?
Which state of matter is best described as one whose particles are tightly packed and can only vibrate about fixed positions?
Which state of matter is best described as one whose particles are far apart and move randomly at high speed?

ma_l1_t1.technicalIntricacy: The three common states of matter differ mainly in how closely their particles are packed and how much freedom those particles have to move, which directly determines whether the substance has a fixed shape, a fixed volume, both, or neither.
ma_l1_t1.realPurpose: Recognising the state of matter from its properties helps explain everyday behaviour, from why gases can be compressed into cylinders to why liquids can be poured but solids cannot.

variants.question: What is the name of the change of state in which a solid turns directly into a gas without becoming a liquid first?
What is the name of the change of state in which a liquid turns into a gas at its surface, below its boiling point?
What is the name of the change of state in which a gas turns into a liquid on cooling?
What is the name of the change of state in which a liquid turns into a solid on cooling?
What is the name of the change of state in which a solid turns into a liquid on heating?

ma_l1_t2.technicalIntricacy: Each change of state has a specific name based on the direction of the transformation and the states involved; these are not random labels but describe exactly how particles gain or lose the energy needed to change their arrangement.
ma_l1_t2.realPurpose: Naming changes of state precisely lets scientists communicate exact processes used in industries such as freeze-drying food, refining crude oil by distillation, and manufacturing dry ice.

variants.question: A substance has a melting point of {{meltingPoint}}°C and a boiling point of {{boilingPoint}}°C. At a temperature of {{temp}}°C, what state of matter will it be in?
distractors: Liquid
Gas
Cannot be determined

variants.question: A substance has a melting point of {{meltingPoint}}°C and a boiling point of {{boilingPoint}}°C. At a temperature of {{midTemp}}°C, what state of matter will it be in?
distractors: Solid
Gas
Cannot be determined

variants.question: A substance has a melting point of {{meltingPoint}}°C and a boiling point of {{boilingPoint}}°C. At a temperature of {{temp}}°C, what state of matter will it be in?
distractors: Solid
Liquid
Cannot be determined

ma_l2_t1.technicalIntricacy: A substance is solid below its melting point, liquid between its melting and boiling points, and gaseous above its boiling point, because temperature directly reflects how much kinetic energy its particles have to overcome the forces holding them together.
ma_l2_t1.realPurpose: This reasoning is used to design refrigeration and heating systems, and to predict how substances will behave when stored or transported at different temperatures.

ma_l2_t2.questionTemplate: A liquid is currently at {{currentTemp}}°C, and its freezing point is {{freezingPoint}}°C. By how many degrees must it cool to reach its freezing point?
ma_l2_t2.technicalIntricacy: The number of degrees a substance must cool to freeze is simply the difference between its current temperature and its freezing point, since temperature falls at a measurable rate until particles slow down enough to lock into a fixed solid arrangement.
ma_l2_t2.realPurpose: This kind of calculation is used in weather forecasting, food storage, and industrial cooling processes to predict exactly when a liquid will solidify.

variants.question: A student heats a beaker of ice and records the temperature every minute. The temperature rises steadily, but then stays constant at 0°C for several minutes even though heating continues, before rising again. Why does the temperature not rise during this period?
variants.answer: The heat energy supplied is being used to melt the ice (break the forces holding particles in place) rather than raise its temperature
distractors: The thermometer must be faulty and is not registering the temperature correctly
The beaker has reached its maximum possible temperature and cannot get any hotter
Heating has stopped reaching the ice because it has formed a protective outer layer

variants.question: A student heats a beaker of boiling water and records the temperature every minute. Once the water starts boiling at 100°C, the temperature stops rising even though heating continues at the same rate. Why does the temperature not rise further?
variants.answer: The heat energy supplied is being used to convert liquid water into steam (break the forces holding particles together) rather than raise its temperature
distractors: The thermometer must be faulty and is not registering the temperature correctly
Water has a fixed maximum temperature it can never exceed under any conditions
The steam produced insulates the water and blocks further heating completely

ma_l3_t1.technicalIntricacy: During a change of state, all the energy supplied goes into overcoming the forces of attraction between particles to rearrange them into a new state, rather than increasing their average kinetic energy (which is what temperature measures) — this hidden energy is called latent heat.
ma_l3_t1.realPurpose: Understanding latent heat explains why steam causes more severe burns than boiling water at the same temperature, and is essential in designing refrigerators, engines and power plants.

variants.question: A bottle of perfume is left open in a room, and soon people far away can smell it even without any wind. On a hot day, this happens noticeably faster than on a cold day. What explains both observations?

An incense stick is left burning in a room, and soon people far away can smell it even without any wind. On a hot day, this happens noticeably faster than on a cold day. What explains both observations?

A pot of food cooking in the kitchen is left uncovered, and soon people far away can smell it even without any wind. On a hot day, this happens noticeably faster than on a cold day. What explains both observations?

ma_l3_t2.answer: Gas particles move randomly and spread out to fill the available space (diffusion), and this spreading speeds up as temperature rises because particles move faster
distractorPool: The smell physically travels only because of air currents caused by people walking nearby
Smell only reaches people because the source object itself is slowly moving through the room
Diffusion only happens in liquids and solids, so temperature has no effect on this scenario
ma_l3_t2.technicalIntricacy: Diffusion is the natural spreading of particles from a region of higher concentration to lower concentration due to their constant random motion; raising the temperature increases the average speed of these particles, so diffusion happens faster.
ma_l3_t2.realPurpose: Diffusion explains how oxygen moves into our blood in the lungs, how food flavours mix, and why gas leaks can be detected from a distance.

variants.question: In which state of matter do particles diffuse (spread out and mix) the fastest?
In which state of matter do particles diffuse the slowest?
What happens to the rate of diffusion as temperature increases?
variants.answer: It increases, since particles move faster

variants.question: What term describes the spontaneous mixing of particles from a region of high concentration to low concentration?

distractorPool: It increases, since particles move faster
ma_l1_t3.technicalIntricacy: Diffusion rate depends directly on how much freedom particles have to move and how fast they're moving; gas particles are far apart and move quickly in every direction, while solid particles are locked in fixed positions and can barely diffuse at all.
ma_l1_t3.realPurpose: Diffusion explains everyday experiences like smelling food from across a room, and its temperature dependence is why smells spread faster on a warm day than a cold one.

variants.question: Which state of matter is easiest to compress (squeeze into a smaller volume)?
Which state of matter is the most difficult to compress?
Why are gases so much easier to compress than liquids or solids?
variants.answer: Because gas particles are far apart, leaving lots of empty space between them

distractorPool: Because gas particles are far apart, leaving lots of empty space between them
Because gas particles are heavier than solid particles
ma_l1_t4.technicalIntricacy: Compressibility depends on how much empty space exists between particles; gases have particles spread far apart with mostly empty space between them, so squeezing a gas mostly just reduces that empty space, while solids and liquids have particles already packed almost as tightly as possible.
ma_l1_t4.realPurpose: This is why gases can be compressed into small cylinders for storage (like cooking gas or oxygen tanks), while liquids and solids strongly resist being squeezed into a smaller volume.

ma_l2_t3.questionTemplate: A substance is heated at a steady rate of {{rate}}°C per minute for {{minutes}} minutes. What is the total rise in temperature?
ma_l2_t3.technicalIntricacy: A steady heating rate means the temperature increases by the same fixed amount every minute, so the total temperature rise is found by multiplying the rate by the total number of minutes.
ma_l2_t3.realPurpose: This kind of calculation is used to predict how long it will take to heat a substance to a target temperature, which is important in cooking, industrial processes, and laboratory experiments.

ma_l2_t4.questionTemplate: A {{initialMass}} g block of solid carbon dioxide (dry ice) sublimates until {{sublimatedPercent}}% of its original mass has turned directly into gas. What mass of solid remains?
ma_l2_t4.technicalIntricacy: Sublimation converts a solid directly into a gas without passing through a liquid state, so the mass lost from the solid is simply the percentage sublimated multiplied by the original mass, and the remaining solid mass is what's left after subtracting that loss.
ma_l2_t4.realPurpose: Understanding sublimation mass loss is useful for tasks like estimating how long dry ice will last during transport and storage of frozen goods.

variants.question: A student notices that a covered pot of boiling water loses much less water overall than an uncovered pot, and concludes that boiling must not really turn water into gas at all when a lid is used. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
variants.answer: Boiling absolutely does turn water into steam (a gas) at the same rate whether the pot is covered or not; the difference is that a lid traps the escaping steam, letting much of it condense back into liquid water on the underside of the lid and drip back in, rather than actually preventing the water from vaporising in the first place
distractors: The student is correct — a covered pot proves that boiling does not actually convert water into a gas at all
A lid works by lowering the boiling point of the water, so far less of it turns into steam
The pot stays fuller only because covering it stops the water from heating up as much in the first place

ma_l3_t3.technicalIntricacy: Boiling continues to produce steam at the same rate under a lid; the lid simply traps that steam in an enclosed space where it cools against the lid's inner surface and condenses back into liquid water, which then drips back into the pot instead of escaping into the surrounding air as it would from an open pot.
ma_l3_t3.realPurpose: This explains why cooking with a lid conserves water and energy — not because less boiling occurs, but because the escaping vapour is recycled back into the pot.

variants.question: A student says a helium balloon shrinks overnight because the helium 'disappears' completely from existence. What is the more accurate, correct explanation?
variants.answer: The helium doesn't disappear — individual helium atoms are small enough to slowly diffuse through the tiny pores in the balloon's rubber material and escape into the surrounding air, where they simply mix with the atmosphere; matter isn't created or destroyed, only spread out and diluted
distractors: The student is correct — the helium atoms are completely destroyed and cease to exist once the balloon shrinks
The balloon shrinks only because the rubber itself physically shrinks over time, with no gas actually escaping
Helium atoms convert into a different, invisible gas inside the balloon, which is why the balloon appears to lose volume

ma_l3_t4.technicalIntricacy: Helium atoms are exceptionally small and light, which lets them gradually diffuse through the microscopic gaps in a balloon's rubber wall over time, escaping into the much larger volume of the surrounding atmosphere, where they become far too dilute to notice, rather than ceasing to exist.
ma_l3_t4.realPurpose: This explains why helium balloons deflate faster than balloons filled with air (made of larger molecules), and reinforces that matter is conserved even when it seems to 'vanish' from a container.

variants.question: At normal atmospheric pressure (sea level), what is the boiling point of pure water?
What is the freezing point (and melting point) of pure water at normal atmospheric pressure?

ma_l1_t5.technicalIntricacy: The boiling and freezing points of pure water are fixed reference values at standard atmospheric pressure — exactly 100°C and 0°C — because they mark the specific temperatures at which water's particles gain or lose enough energy to change state.
ma_l1_t5.realPurpose: These two fixed points are so reliable that they were historically used to define the Celsius temperature scale itself, and they remain essential reference values throughout science and everyday life.

variants.question: Unlike boiling, which happens throughout an entire liquid at one fixed temperature, evaporation can happen at any temperature — but only from where in the liquid?
variants.answer: Only from the exposed surface of the liquid
distractors: Throughout the entire liquid, exactly like boiling
Only from the very bottom of the container
Only when the liquid is completely still

variants.question: Does evaporation of a liquid (such as water drying from a wet floor) require the liquid to be heated all the way to its boiling point?
variants.answer: No, evaporation can happen slowly at any temperature, even well below the boiling point
distractors: Yes, evaporation can only occur once the liquid reaches its exact boiling point
Yes, but only if the liquid is first frozen and then heated
No, evaporation only happens below 0°C

ma_l1_t6.technicalIntricacy: Evaporation is a surface phenomenon that can occur at any temperature, because a few high-energy particles at the surface always have enough energy to escape as gas, while boiling requires the entire liquid to reach a specific temperature at which particles throughout the liquid gain enough energy to turn to gas.
ma_l1_t6.realPurpose: This distinction explains why a puddle can dry up on a cool day without ever boiling, and why boiling is a much faster, more energetic process confined to a specific temperature.

variants.question: Does increasing the temperature of a liquid generally speed up or slow down its rate of evaporation?
variants.answer: Speed it up, since particles gain more energy and escape faster
distractors: Slow it down, since particles move more slowly at higher temperatures
Have no effect at all on the rate of evaporation
Only affect boiling, never evaporation

variants.question: Does increasing the exposed surface area of a liquid generally speed up or slow down its rate of evaporation?
variants.answer: Speed it up, since more particles are exposed at the surface and can escape
distractors: Slow it down, since a larger surface traps particles more effectively
Have no effect at all on the rate of evaporation
Only affect boiling, never evaporation

variants.question: Does blowing air across the surface of a liquid generally speed up or slow down its rate of evaporation?
variants.answer: Speed it up, since moving air carries away escaped particles and lets more evaporate
distractors: Slow it down, since moving air pushes escaping particles back into the liquid
Have no effect at all on the rate of evaporation
Only affect boiling, never evaporation

ma_l1_t7.technicalIntricacy: The rate of evaporation increases whenever particles at the surface gain more energy (higher temperature), have more room to escape from (larger surface area), or have their escape route kept clear of returning particles (moving air), since these all make it easier for particles to leave the liquid and become gas.
ma_l1_t7.realPurpose: Understanding these factors explains everyday observations, like why wet clothes dry faster on a hot, windy day when spread out flat rather than bunched up.

variants.question: What is the name of the scientific theory stating that all matter is made up of tiny particles that are constantly moving?
variants.answer: The kinetic particle theory (kinetic theory of matter)

variants.question: According to the kinetic particle theory, what generally happens to the speed of a substance's particles as its temperature increases?
variants.answer: The particles move faster, on average

distractorPool: The kinetic particle theory (kinetic theory of matter)
The particles move faster, on average
The law of conservation of mass
ma_l1_t8.technicalIntricacy: The kinetic particle theory is the foundational model explaining almost all behaviour of matter — it states that particles in every state of matter are always in motion, and that raising the temperature increases their average energy and speed.
ma_l1_t8.realPurpose: This theory underlies the explanation for every change of state, diffusion, and pressure effect covered in this chapter, making it one of the most important ideas in introductory chemistry.

variants.question: Because their particles are the most tightly packed, which state of matter is generally the most dense?
Because their particles are spread so far apart, which state of matter is generally the least dense?

ma_l1_t9.technicalIntricacy: Density depends on how much mass is packed into a given volume; since solids generally have their particles packed closest together and gases have theirs spread furthest apart, solids are usually the densest state and gases the least dense, with liquids in between (water and ice are a well-known exception to this general trend).
ma_l1_t9.realPurpose: Understanding this general density trend explains why gases can be so easily compressed compared to liquids or solids, and why solids usually sink in their own melted liquid form.

variants.question: Between melting and freezing, which change of state occurs when a substance is heated?
Between boiling and condensation, which change of state occurs when a substance is heated?
Between freezing and condensation, which change of state occurs when a substance is cooled and turns into a solid?
Between evaporation and condensation, which change of state occurs when a substance is cooled and turns into a liquid?

ma_l1_t10.technicalIntricacy: Changes of state can be grouped by whether they require adding heat energy (melting and boiling/evaporation) or removing it (freezing and condensation), since particles need extra energy to break free into a more disordered state and must lose energy to settle into a more ordered one.
ma_l1_t10.realPurpose: Grouping changes of state by heating versus cooling makes it easy to predict which direction a process will go, which is essential in designing heating and cooling systems.

ma_l2_t5.questionTemplate: A sample of ice starts at {{startTemp}}°C and is heated steadily at {{rate}}°C per minute. How many minutes will it take for the ice to reach its melting point of 0°C?
ma_l2_t5.technicalIntricacy: Since the ice must warm up steadily from its starting (negative) temperature to 0°C, the time required is simply the total temperature rise needed divided by the fixed heating rate per minute.
ma_l2_t5.realPurpose: This kind of calculation helps predict exactly how long it will take frozen food or ice samples to reach a target temperature under steady heating, which matters in food safety and laboratory work.

variants.question: Is the melting of ice into water a physical change or a chemical change?
Is the burning of paper a physical change or a chemical change?
Is the rusting of an iron nail a physical change or a chemical change?
Is cutting a piece of cloth into two pieces a physical change or a chemical change?
Is the boiling of water into steam a physical change or a chemical change?
Is the digestion of food in the stomach a physical change or a chemical change?
Is dissolving salt in water a physical change or a chemical change?
Is the souring of milk a physical change or a chemical change?

distractorPool: Neither a physical nor a chemical change
Both a physical and a chemical change simultaneously
ch_l1_t1.technicalIntricacy: A physical change only alters a substance's size, shape or state without changing its chemical composition, while a chemical change breaks and forms chemical bonds to create one or more entirely new substances with different properties.
ch_l1_t1.realPurpose: Correctly classifying changes helps predict whether a process can be reversed, which is essential in recycling, cooking, and manufacturing.

variants.question: During an experiment, bubbles of gas form as soon as two substances are mixed together. What sign of a chemical change does this observation indicate?
During an experiment, the mixture becomes noticeably hotter immediately after two substances are combined. What sign of a chemical change does this observation indicate?
During an experiment, a cloudy solid settles at the bottom after two clear solutions are mixed. What sign of a chemical change does this observation indicate?
During an experiment, a colourless solution turns bright blue after a piece of metal is added to it. What sign of a chemical change does this observation indicate?

distractorPool: The total mass increases without limit
ch_l1_t2.technicalIntricacy: Chemical reactions are usually detected by observable evidence — such as gas bubbles, heat or light release, a colour change, or a precipitate — because these all indicate that new substances with different properties have formed.
ch_l1_t2.realPurpose: Recognising these signs lets chemists confirm that a reaction has actually taken place, which is essential in laboratory analysis and industrial quality control.

ch_l2_t1.questionTemplate: {{massA}} g of substance A reacts completely with {{massB}} g of substance B in a sealed container. According to the Law of Conservation of Mass, what is the total mass of the products formed?
ch_l2_t1.technicalIntricacy: The Law of Conservation of Mass states that mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction; in a sealed system, the total mass of the reactants must exactly equal the total mass of the products.
ch_l2_t1.realPurpose: This law is the basis for balancing chemical equations and for accurately calculating the yield of products in industrial chemical manufacturing.

ch_l2_t2.questionTemplate: An iron nail of mass {{ironMass}} g rusts completely, chemically combining with {{oxygenMass}} g of oxygen from the air. What is the total mass of the rust (iron oxide) formed?
ch_l2_t2.technicalIntricacy: Rusting is a chemical change in which iron atoms combine with oxygen atoms from the air; because oxygen is added to the solid rather than escaping as a gas, the mass of the rust formed is greater than the mass of the original iron.
ch_l2_t2.realPurpose: This surprising mass increase is a clear demonstration that rusting is a genuine chemical reaction, not just surface wear, and explains why rusted metal structures can weigh more before they eventually crumble away.

variants.question: A student burns a piece of paper completely and weighs the leftover ash, finding it weighs much less than the original object. The student concludes that mass has been destroyed. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
variants.answer: The missing mass escaped into the air as gases (like carbon dioxide and water vapour) that were not weighed, so no mass was actually destroyed
distractors: Mass truly was destroyed, proving the Law of Conservation of Mass does not apply to burning
The weighing scale must have malfunctioned during the second measurement
Burning removes mass by converting it directly into heat energy with no matter left over

ch_l3_t1.technicalIntricacy: Combustion produces gaseous products such as carbon dioxide and water vapour that escape into the surrounding air; if these escaping gases were captured and weighed along with the ash, the total mass would exactly equal the original mass of the burned object plus the oxygen it reacted with.
ch_l3_t1.realPurpose: This misconception, once corrected, reinforces the universal validity of the Law of Conservation of Mass and explains why chemists must work with sealed systems to verify it experimentally.

variants.question: A student watches a wax candle melt and argues this must be a chemical change because "it turned into something completely different." What is wrong with this reasoning?
variants.answer: Melting is a physical change — the substance is still made of the same molecules, no new substance formed, and it would return to its original solid form on cooling
distractors: The student is correct, because anything that changes its appearance has undergone a chemical change
It is impossible to classify this change without first testing its chemical composition in a laboratory
It must be a chemical change because heat was involved in causing the transformation

ch_l3_t2.technicalIntricacy: Melting only supplies enough energy to overcome the forces holding particles in a fixed solid arrangement, allowing them to move past one another as a liquid; the chemical identity and composition of the substance's molecules remain completely unchanged throughout.
ch_l3_t2.realPurpose: Distinguishing a change in appearance from a change in chemical identity is essential for correctly identifying reversible processes like melting, which can be undone, from irreversible chemical reactions.

variants.question: Is melting chocolate that can be cooled back into a solid bar a reversible or an irreversible change?
Is baking a cake from batter a reversible or an irreversible change?
Is folding a piece of paper into an origami shape a reversible or an irreversible change?
Is burning a piece of paper to ash a reversible or an irreversible change?
Is freezing water into ice cubes a reversible or an irreversible change?
Is cooking a raw egg into a fried egg a reversible or an irreversible change?

distractorPool: Neither a physical nor a chemical change
A change that has no cause or effect
ch_l1_t3.technicalIntricacy: Reversible changes can generally be undone to restore the original substance, most often because they're physical changes, while irreversible changes usually cannot be undone because a genuinely new substance has formed through a chemical reaction.
ch_l1_t3.realPurpose: Recognising reversibility helps predict whether a process (like recycling metal or freezing food) can restore an original material, or whether it permanently transforms it (like cooking or burning).

variants.question: What term describes a chemical reaction that releases heat into the surroundings?
What term describes a chemical reaction that absorbs heat from the surroundings?
Is burning (combustion) generally an exothermic or an endothermic reaction?

ch_l1_t4.technicalIntricacy: Chemical reactions either release stored chemical energy as heat (exothermic) or absorb heat energy from their surroundings to proceed (endothermic), and this energy flow is often noticeable as the reacting mixture heating up or cooling down.
ch_l1_t4.realPurpose: Recognising exothermic and endothermic reactions explains everyday phenomena, from a hand warmer heating up (exothermic) to an instant cold pack cooling down (endothermic).

ch_l2_t3.questionTemplate: {{massA}} g of substance A, {{massB}} g of substance B, and {{massC}} g of substance C react completely to form a single new compound in a sealed container. According to the Law of Conservation of Mass, what is the total mass of the compound formed?
ch_l2_t3.technicalIntricacy: The Law of Conservation of Mass applies no matter how many reactants are involved — the combined mass of every reactant must exactly equal the mass of the product(s) formed, as long as the reaction occurs in a sealed system.
ch_l2_t3.realPurpose: This principle scales up directly to real industrial chemistry, where manufacturers must account for every raw ingredient's mass to accurately predict how much product a reaction will yield.

ch_l2_t4.questionTemplate: An iron object of mass {{ironMass}} g rusts, and its mass increases by {{percentGain}}% as it combines with oxygen from the air. What is the mass of the rusted object?
ch_l2_t4.technicalIntricacy: Since rusting adds oxygen atoms onto the iron rather than releasing any gas, the rusted object's final mass equals the original iron mass plus the added mass from the oxygen it absorbed, calculated here as a percentage increase.
ch_l2_t4.realPurpose: This mass-gain calculation reinforces why rusting is a genuine chemical reaction rather than simple wear, since the object measurably gains mass instead of losing it.

variants.question: A student mixes vinegar and baking soda, observes fizzing bubbles, but insists nothing chemical happened because "no smoke or fire was involved." What is the flaw in this reasoning?
variants.answer: Fizzing or bubbling (gas production) is itself one of the clear signs of a chemical reaction; a chemical change doesn't require fire or smoke — the production of a new gas shows that new substances have formed, meeting the definition of a chemical reaction regardless of the absence of flames
distractors: The student is correct — a chemical reaction can only be confirmed if fire, smoke, or an explosion is directly observed
The bubbles are just air being physically released from the liquids, unrelated to any chemical process
This reaction is only chemical if the bubbles are a specific colour, such as blue or green

ch_l3_t3.technicalIntricacy: When vinegar (an acid) reacts with baking soda (a base), they produce carbon dioxide gas along with water and a new dissolved salt; the visible fizzing is direct evidence of this new gas being produced, which is a textbook sign of a chemical reaction, entirely independent of whether fire or smoke is present.
ch_l3_t3.realPurpose: Recognising gas production as a sign of chemical change (not just fire or smoke) is essential for correctly identifying countless everyday chemical reactions, from baking to cleaning products reacting together.

variants.question: A student assumes that any process producing a colour change must be a chemical change, and classifies mixing two paint colours together (like blue and yellow to make green) as a chemical reaction. What is the mistake in this reasoning?
variants.answer: Mixing paints to blend a new colour is a physical change, not a chemical reaction — the paint particles are simply mixed together without any new substance being chemically formed; a colour change is a common SIGN of a chemical reaction, but it isn't proof by itself
distractors: The student is correct — any change in colour, for any reason, is always definitive proof that a chemical reaction has occurred
Mixing paint colours is a nuclear change, not a physical or chemical one
Blending paint colours only counts as a chemical reaction if the resulting colour is unexpected or surprising

ch_l3_t4.technicalIntricacy: Blending paint colours simply combines existing pigment particles physically, without any chemical bonds breaking or forming to create a genuinely new substance; while a colour change is often associated with chemical reactions, it can also occur from purely physical mixing, so it must be considered alongside other evidence rather than on its own.
ch_l3_t4.realPurpose: This distinction prevents a very common mix-up, and highlights that no single sign alone (colour change, temperature change, etc.) is always sufficient proof of a chemical reaction by itself.

variants.question: Milk that has gone sour develops a strong, unpleasant new smell. What sign of a chemical change does this observation indicate?
During a reaction, an unfamiliar new smell appears in a mixture that had no smell before it was combined. What sign of a chemical change does this observation indicate?

ch_l1_t5.technicalIntricacy: A new, unfamiliar smell appearing during a reaction is another reliable sign that new substances (with their own distinct odours) have formed, alongside the other classic signs of a chemical change like gas, colour, precipitate and temperature changes.
ch_l1_t5.realPurpose: Recognising smell as a genuine sign of chemical change helps identify reactions like food spoiling, alongside more visually obvious signs like bubbling or colour change.

variants.question: For an iron nail to rust, which two substances must BOTH be present?
Will a dry iron nail kept in a sealed container of pure, moisture-free oxygen rust quickly?
variants.answer: No, because rusting also requires moisture (water) to be present, not just oxygen

distractorPool: No, because rusting also requires moisture (water) to be present, not just oxygen
Only oxygen is needed, water plays no role at all
Only water is needed, oxygen plays no role at all
ch_l1_t6.technicalIntricacy: Rusting is a chemical reaction between iron, oxygen and water together; without moisture present, iron reacts with oxygen far too slowly to visibly rust, which is why rusting is so much faster and more severe in humid or wet conditions.
ch_l1_t6.realPurpose: This is exactly why keeping iron and steel objects dry (through paint, oil or galvanising) is one of the most effective ways to prevent rusting.

variants.question: Besides releasing heat and light, what does the complete combustion (burning) of a fuel like wood or paper typically produce?
variants.answer: Ash, along with gases such as carbon dioxide and water vapour

variants.question: What gas from the air is essential for combustion to take place at all?

distractorPool: Ash, along with gases such as carbon dioxide and water vapour
Only pure carbon and nothing else
Only water and no other substances
ch_l1_t7.technicalIntricacy: Combustion is a chemical reaction between a fuel and oxygen from the air; it releases energy as heat and light, while producing new substances — typically ash (leftover solid material) plus gases like carbon dioxide and water vapour that escape into the air.
ch_l1_t7.realPurpose: Knowing what combustion actually produces (not just 'fire') is essential for understanding air pollution from burning fuels and for calculating the mass balance of a combustion reaction.

variants.question: Is dissolving sugar completely in a cup of water a physical change or a chemical change?
After sugar is dissolved in water, can it be recovered largely unchanged by evaporating away the water?
variants.answer: Yes, since dissolving is a physical change and no new substance was formed

distractorPool: Yes, since dissolving is a physical change and no new substance was formed
No, because dissolving permanently destroys the sugar
ch_l1_t8.technicalIntricacy: When sugar or salt dissolves in water, its particles simply spread out and mix evenly with the water particles without any new chemical bonds forming, so the dissolved substance can always be recovered essentially unchanged by evaporating the water away.
ch_l1_t8.realPurpose: Recognising dissolving as a physical (not chemical) change explains why we can recover salt from seawater by evaporation, and why sugar dissolved in tea can still be tasted as sugar.

variants.question: Is photosynthesis (where plants use sunlight to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen) a physical change or a chemical change?

distractorPool: Neither a physical nor a chemical change
Both a physical and a chemical change simultaneously
ch_l1_t9.technicalIntricacy: Photosynthesis is a chemical change because it converts carbon dioxide and water into entirely new substances — glucose and oxygen — with completely different properties, using light energy to drive the reaction rather than heat.
ch_l1_t9.realPurpose: Recognising photosynthesis as a chemical reaction highlights that chemical changes aren't always about burning or fire — some, like photosynthesis, absorb light energy to build up new substances instead.

variants.question: What term describes a change that produces one or more brand new substances with different properties from the original?
What term describes a change that only alters the size, shape or state of a substance, without forming any new substance?

ch_l1_t10.technicalIntricacy: These two definitions are the foundation for classifying every change in matter: a chemical change always creates new substances with different properties, while a physical change never does, regardless of how dramatic the change looks.
ch_l1_t10.realPurpose: Being able to state these definitions precisely (rather than relying only on examples) allows correctly classifying changes never seen before, based on first principles.

ch_l2_t5.questionTemplate: A candle of mass {{candleMass}} g burns completely, combining with {{oxygenMass}} g of oxygen from the air to form carbon dioxide gas and water vapour (both of which escape into the air). According to the Law of Conservation of Mass, what is the total mass of the gaseous products formed?
ch_l2_t5.technicalIntricacy: Even though the candle appears to shrink and 'disappear,' the Law of Conservation of Mass still holds: the wax combines with oxygen from the air, so the total mass of the escaping gaseous products equals the mass of the candle wax burned plus the mass of oxygen it reacted with.
ch_l2_t5.realPurpose: This calculation explains why burned objects seem to lose mass when only weighed as solid leftovers — the 'missing' mass has escaped as gas, not vanished, which is essential for understanding combustion in sealed-system experiments.

variants.question: Is oxygen gas an element, a compound, or a mixture?
Is iron an element, a compound, or a mixture?
Is gold an element, a compound, or a mixture?
Is water (H₂O) an element, a compound, or a mixture?
Is carbon dioxide (CO₂) an element, a compound, or a mixture?
Is table salt (NaCl) an element, a compound, or a mixture?
Is air an element, a compound, or a mixture?
Is salt water an element, a compound, or a mixture?
Is a mixture of sand and iron filings an element, a compound, or a mixture?

mx_l1_t1.technicalIntricacy: Elements contain only one type of atom, compounds contain two or more elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio, and mixtures contain two or more substances that are simply combined physically without any fixed ratio or chemical bonding.
mx_l1_t1.realPurpose: This classification determines how a substance can be broken down or purified — elements cannot be simplified further, compounds require a chemical reaction, and mixtures can be separated by physical methods.

variants.question: Which method would be most suitable for separating insoluble chalk powder from water?
Which method would be most suitable for recovering dissolved salt from salt water by removing all the water?
Which method would be most suitable for separating pure water from salt water while also collecting the water itself?
Which method would be most suitable for separating iron filings that are mixed with sand?
Which method would be most suitable for separating camphor from a mixture with sand?

mx_l1_t2.technicalIntricacy: Each separation technique exploits a specific physical difference between the components of a mixture — particle size for filtration, boiling point for evaporation and distillation, magnetism for magnetic separation, and the ability to sublime for sublimation.
mx_l1_t2.realPurpose: Choosing the correct separation method is essential in water purification, mining, recycling, and everyday laboratory practice.

mx_l2_t1.questionTemplate: Water (H₂O) always contains hydrogen and oxygen combined in a fixed mass ratio of 1 : 8. If a sample of water contains {{hydrogenMass}} g of hydrogen, what mass of oxygen must it contain?
mx_l2_t1.technicalIntricacy: Because water is a compound, its elements are always combined in the exact same fixed mass ratio, no matter how large or small the sample is — this fixed ratio is what distinguishes a compound from a mixture, where proportions can vary freely.
mx_l2_t1.realPurpose: Fixed combining ratios allow chemists to calculate exactly how much of each raw element is needed to manufacture a required amount of a compound.

mx_l2_t2.questionTemplate: Magnesium oxide always contains magnesium and oxygen combined in a fixed mass ratio of 3 : 2. If a sample of magnesium oxide contains {{magnesiumMass}} g of magnesium, what mass of oxygen must it contain?
mx_l2_t2.technicalIntricacy: A fixed mass ratio in a compound reflects the fixed whole-number ratio of atoms combining at the microscopic level; scaling the sample size up or down never changes this underlying ratio.
mx_l2_t2.realPurpose: Understanding fixed ratios in compounds is essential for balancing chemical equations and for quality-controlling manufactured chemical products.

variants.question: A student mixes iron filings and sulfur powder together and claims this must be a compound because 'the two substances are now combined.' A classmate disagrees. Who is correct, and why?
variants.answer: It is a mixture, not a compound, because iron and sulfur are only physically combined and can still be separated using a magnet, unlike a true compound
distractors: It is a compound, because once two substances are combined they always form a compound automatically
It cannot be classified as either a mixture or a compound without first melting it
It is an element, since both iron and sulfur individually are already elements

mx_l3_t1.technicalIntricacy: Simply physically combining substances does not create a compound; a compound only forms through a chemical reaction that chemically bonds elements in a fixed ratio, producing a new substance with entirely different properties, such as iron sulfide formed by heating iron and sulfur together.
mx_l3_t1.realPurpose: This classic experiment demonstrates the key difference between mixtures and compounds, since the iron in the mixture still responds to a magnet while iron combined chemically in iron sulfide does not.

variants.question: A student tries to separate a mixture of alcohol and water by pouring it through filter paper, but the same liquid mixture passes straight through unchanged. What is wrong with the student's approach?

A student tries to separate a mixture of vinegar and water by pouring it through filter paper, but the same liquid mixture passes straight through unchanged. What is wrong with the student's approach?
A student tries to separate a mixture of milk and water by pouring it through filter paper, but the same liquid mixture passes straight through unchanged. What is wrong with the student's approach?

mx_l3_t2.answer: Filtration only separates an insoluble solid from a liquid; since both liquids mix completely (are miscible), filtration cannot separate them and distillation must be used instead
distractorPool: The filter paper used must have had holes that were too large for this particular mixture
The mixture needed to be heated to a very high temperature before filtration could work
Filtration works perfectly for any two liquids as long as they are stirred thoroughly beforehand
mx_l3_t2.technicalIntricacy: Filtration relies on a physical size difference between solid particles and the liquid they are suspended in; when two substances are both liquids that mix completely at a molecular level, there are no solid particles for the filter paper to trap.
mx_l3_t2.realPurpose: Recognising which separation method suits which mixture is essential in real laboratory and industrial processes, such as distilling alcohol or purifying water.

variants.question: In a solution of salt water, what term describes the salt (the substance being dissolved)?
In a solution of salt water, what term describes the water (the substance doing the dissolving)?
What term describes a solution that has dissolved as much solute as it possibly can at a given temperature?

mx_l1_t3.technicalIntricacy: Every solution is made of a solvent (the larger-quantity substance doing the dissolving) and one or more solutes (the substances being dissolved); a saturated solution is one where the solvent has reached its limit and can't dissolve any more solute at that temperature.
mx_l1_t3.realPurpose: This vocabulary is essential for describing solutions precisely, from mixing a hot drink to understanding how much salt the ocean can dissolve at different temperatures.

variants.question: Are oil and water miscible or immiscible liquids?
Are alcohol and water miscible or immiscible liquids?
Are vinegar and water miscible or immiscible liquids?
Are petrol and water miscible or immiscible liquids?

distractorPool: A pure compound, not a mixture of two liquids at all
A solid mixture, not a liquid one
mx_l1_t4.technicalIntricacy: Whether two liquids mix depends on how similar their molecules are; liquids with similar molecular structures (like alcohol and water) mix completely (miscible), while very different ones (like oil and water) separate into distinct layers instead (immiscible).
mx_l1_t4.realPurpose: Recognising miscibility determines how a liquid mixture can be separated — immiscible liquids can be separated using a separating funnel, while miscible ones require distillation.

mx_l2_t3.questionTemplate: {{soluteMass}} g of salt is dissolved completely in {{solventMass}} g of water. What percentage of the total solution's mass is salt?
mx_l2_t3.technicalIntricacy: The percentage of solute in a solution is found by dividing the solute's mass by the total mass of the whole solution (solute plus solvent combined), then multiplying by 100.
mx_l2_t3.realPurpose: This kind of concentration calculation is used constantly in cooking, medicine dosing, and industrial chemistry, wherever a precise strength of solution is required.

mx_l2_t4.questionTemplate: A separating funnel contains {{totalVolume}} mL of a mixture of oil and water, in which oil makes up {{oilPercent}}% of the total volume. What volume of water is in the mixture?
mx_l2_t4.technicalIntricacy: Since oil and water are immiscible and their percentages must add up to the total volume, the water's volume is found by subtracting the oil's volume (calculated from its percentage) from the total mixture volume.
mx_l2_t4.realPurpose: This kind of calculation is directly useful when using a separating funnel, where knowing the expected volume of each layer helps confirm the separation was done correctly.

variants.question: A student tries to separate sugar dissolved in water using a magnet, reasoning that 'magnets can separate anything.' What is the mistake in this reasoning?
variants.answer: Magnets only attract magnetic materials like iron, cobalt and nickel; sugar is not magnetic at all, so a magnet has zero effect on separating dissolved sugar from water — evaporation (or distillation, to recover the water too) is the correct method for this particular mixture
distractors: The student is correct — magnets are a universal separation tool that works on any mixture, including dissolved sugar and water
Magnets can separate sugar from water, but only if the water is boiling hot at the time
Sugar water cannot be separated by any method once the sugar has fully dissolved

mx_l3_t3.technicalIntricacy: Magnetic separation works only because certain materials (like iron) respond to a magnetic field due to their specific atomic structure; sugar, being a non-magnetic organic compound, has no magnetic properties whatsoever, so no magnet, no matter how strong, will have any effect on it.
mx_l3_t3.realPurpose: Understanding that each separation technique relies on a specific physical property (magnetism, boiling point, particle size, etc.) prevents mismatching a technique to a mixture it simply cannot work on.

variants.question: A student assumes that a solution which looks completely clear (with no visible particles) cannot possibly contain a dissolved solid, reasoning that 'if something was in there, I'd be able to see it.' What is the flaw in this reasoning?
variants.answer: A properly dissolved solute breaks down into particles far too small to see with the naked eye, and spreads evenly throughout the solvent — this is exactly why solutions appear clear and uniform even though they definitely do contain dissolved material; visibility is not a reliable test for whether something is dissolved
distractors: The student is correct — if a solution looks completely clear, it is guaranteed to contain no dissolved solids at all
Clear solutions can only ever contain dissolved gases, never dissolved solids
The clarity of a solution depends entirely on its temperature, not on whether anything is dissolved in it

mx_l3_t4.technicalIntricacy: When a solid solute dissolves, it breaks apart into individual molecules or ions that are thousands of times smaller than the wavelength of visible light, meaning they simply cannot scatter light the way larger suspended particles do — this is precisely why solutions look transparent while still containing genuinely dissolved material.
mx_l3_t4.realPurpose: Understanding this helps explain why simple visual inspection cannot confirm water purity, which is why real water testing relies on chemical tests rather than just looking at a sample.

variants.question: In a mixture like salt water, where the dissolved particles are far too small to see and never settle out, what type of mixture is this called?
Is a true solution (like sugar dissolved in water) generally clear and transparent, or cloudy?

mx_l1_t5.technicalIntricacy: A solution is a mixture where the solute's particles are broken down so small (at the molecular or ionic level) that they spread completely evenly through the solvent, never settle out on standing, and don't scatter light, which is why solutions look clear.
mx_l1_t5.realPurpose: Recognising true solutions helps distinguish them from suspensions and colloids, which look and behave very differently despite all being mixtures.

variants.question: In a mixture like muddy water, where relatively large particles are visibly suspended and settle to the bottom on standing, what type of mixture is this called?
Will the particles in a suspension (like chalk powder shaken in water) eventually settle out if left undisturbed?
variants.answer: Yes, given enough time, the particles will settle to the bottom

distractorPool: Yes, given enough time, the particles will settle to the bottom
No, they will remain evenly mixed forever
mx_l1_t6.technicalIntricacy: A suspension contains relatively large, visible particles that are only temporarily held up by the liquid; because these particles are much bigger than the particles in a true solution, gravity eventually pulls them down to settle at the bottom once the mixture is left undisturbed.
mx_l1_t6.realPurpose: Recognising suspensions is important in everyday situations, from muddy water needing to settle or be filtered, to medicines that must be shaken before use because their ingredients settle over time.

variants.question: Milk and fog are examples of mixtures where the particles are too small to settle out on their own, but too large to form a true solution — what type of mixture is this called?

mx_l1_t7.technicalIntricacy: A colloid contains particles that are intermediate in size between those in a true solution and a suspension; these particles are small enough to stay evenly spread out without settling, but large enough to scatter light, which is why colloids like milk or fog often appear cloudy rather than perfectly clear.
mx_l1_t7.realPurpose: Recognising colloids explains why substances like milk, fog and gelatin look cloudy without ever settling into layers, unlike suspensions that eventually separate.

variants.question: Which separation technique is most suitable for separating different coloured dyes mixed together in a single ink sample?
What physical property does chromatography rely on to separate substances dissolved together in a mixture?
variants.answer: Differences in how easily each substance moves through (or dissolves in) a particular material, such as paper

distractorPool: Differences in how easily each substance moves through (or dissolves in) a particular material, such as paper
Differences in magnetism between the substances
mx_l1_t8.technicalIntricacy: Chromatography separates dissolved substances in a mixture by exploiting small differences in how strongly each one is attracted to (or moves through) a material such as paper, so components that move faster spread further, separating the mixture into distinct bands.
mx_l1_t8.realPurpose: Chromatography is widely used to identify and separate the components of inks and food dyes, and even to detect banned substances in forensic and sports drug testing.

variants.question: What term describes a solution that can still dissolve more solute at its current temperature?
If a solution is unsaturated, does it mean the solvent has reached its maximum dissolving capacity, or that it can still dissolve more solute?
variants.answer: It can still dissolve more solute

distractorPool: It can still dissolve more solute
It has reached its maximum dissolving capacity
mx_l1_t9.technicalIntricacy: An unsaturated solution is simply one that hasn't yet reached the maximum amount of solute its solvent can dissolve at that temperature, meaning more solute can still be added and will continue to dissolve.
mx_l1_t9.realPurpose: Distinguishing saturated from unsaturated solutions matters in situations like crystallisation, where a solution must first become saturated before extra solute will form solid crystals instead of dissolving.

variants.question: Can filtration be used to separate the particles of a suspension (like chalk powder in water) from the liquid?
variants.answer: Yes, because the particles are large enough to be trapped by filter paper

variants.question: Can filtration be used to separate the dissolved particles of a true solution (like salt fully dissolved in water) from the liquid?
variants.answer: No, because the dissolved particles are far too small to be trapped by filter paper

distractorPool: Yes, because the particles are large enough to be trapped by filter paper
No, because the dissolved particles are far too small to be trapped by filter paper
Yes, filtration works equally well on both suspensions and true solutions
No, filtration cannot separate any kind of mixture at all
mx_l1_t10.technicalIntricacy: Filtration works only when the particles being removed are physically larger than the pores in the filter paper; a suspension's relatively large particles are trapped easily, while a true solution's particles are dissolved at the molecular level and pass straight through with the liquid.
mx_l1_t10.realPurpose: This distinction is exactly why filtration can clear up muddy (suspended) water but cannot remove dissolved salt from seawater, where evaporation or distillation must be used instead.

mx_l2_t5.questionTemplate: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) always contains carbon and oxygen combined in a fixed mass ratio of 3 : 8. If a sample of carbon dioxide contains {{carbonMass}} g of carbon, what mass of oxygen must it contain?
mx_l2_t5.technicalIntricacy: A fixed mass ratio in a compound reflects the fixed whole-number ratio of atoms combining at the microscopic level; scaling the sample size up or down never changes this underlying ratio, whether the compound is water, magnesium oxide, or carbon dioxide.
mx_l2_t5.realPurpose: Being able to apply fixed combining ratios to different compounds is essential for chemists calculating exactly how much of each raw element is needed to manufacture a required amount of any compound.

variants.question: Which subatomic particle carries a positive charge and is found inside the nucleus?
Which subatomic particle carries a negative charge and moves around the nucleus in shells?
Which subatomic particle carries no electrical charge and is found inside the nucleus?

at_l1_t1.technicalIntricacy: Protons and neutrons together make up the small, dense nucleus at the centre of an atom, while much lighter electrons occupy the much larger surrounding space in shells, held in place by their electrical attraction to the positively charged protons.
at_l1_t1.realPurpose: Knowing the charge and location of each subatomic particle explains how atoms form chemical bonds, conduct electricity, and interact with radiation.

variants.question: The atomic number of an atom is defined as the number of ___ in its nucleus.
distractors: Neutrons
Protons and neutrons combined
Electrons in the outermost shell only

variants.question: The mass number of an atom is defined as the total number of ___ in its nucleus.
distractors: Protons only
Neutrons only
Protons, neutrons and electrons combined

at_l1_t2.technicalIntricacy: Atomic number identifies an element by counting only its protons, while mass number accounts for the total number of heavy particles (protons and neutrons) in the nucleus, since electrons contribute negligible mass.
at_l1_t2.realPurpose: These two numbers together let scientists identify any atom precisely, calculate its approximate mass, and predict how many electrons it has when neutral.

at_l2_t1.questionTemplate: An atom has an atomic number of {{protons}} and a mass number of {{massNumber}}. How many neutrons does it contain?
at_l2_t1.technicalIntricacy: Since mass number equals the total of protons and neutrons, the number of neutrons is found by subtracting the atomic number (protons) from the mass number.
at_l2_t1.realPurpose: This calculation is used to identify isotopes of an element, which are atoms with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.

at_l2_t2.questionTemplate: An atom contains {{protons}} protons and {{neutrons}} neutrons in its nucleus. What is its mass number?
at_l2_t2.technicalIntricacy: Mass number is simply the sum of the protons and neutrons in the nucleus, since these two particles account for almost all of an atom's total mass.
at_l2_t2.realPurpose: Mass number is used to label isotopes (for example, carbon-12 and carbon-14) and to calculate an element's approximate atomic mass.

variants.question: A student says that an atom with an atomic number of {{atomicNumber}} must have {{atomicNumber}} neutrons, since "atomic number tells you the particles in the nucleus that aren't electrons." What is the mistake in this reasoning?
variants.answer: Atomic number tells you the number of protons (which also equals the number of electrons in a neutral atom), not the number of neutrons
distractors: The student is correct, since atomic number directly counts every particle inside the nucleus that is not a proton
Atomic number only applies to elements with an even number of protons
Neutron count can never be determined for any atom, with or without the atomic number

at_l3_t1.technicalIntricacy: Atomic number is defined specifically as the number of protons in the nucleus; to find the number of neutrons, you must separately subtract the atomic number from the mass number, since neutron count is not fixed for a given element (different isotopes have different neutron numbers).
at_l3_t1.realPurpose: Avoiding this confusion is essential for correctly identifying elements and their isotopes on the periodic table.

variants.question: A student examines an atom with {{equalCount}} protons and {{equalCount}} electrons and concludes it must be electrically charged (an ion) because it contains "two different types of particles." What is wrong with this reasoning?
variants.answer: Having equal numbers of protons and electrons makes the atom electrically neutral, not charged; an atom only becomes an ion when protons and electrons are unequal
distractors: The student is correct, since having two different types of particles always means an object is electrically charged
The atom is negatively charged because electrons are being counted at all
The atom's charge cannot be determined without also knowing its number of neutrons

at_l3_t2.technicalIntricacy: Each proton's positive charge is exactly balanced by each electron's negative charge; as long as the number of protons equals the number of electrons, their charges cancel out completely, leaving the atom electrically neutral overall.
at_l3_t2.realPurpose: Understanding this balance explains why atoms are normally neutral and how they become positively or negatively charged ions by losing or gaining electrons during chemical reactions.

variants.question: What is the maximum number of electrons that can occupy the first (innermost) electron shell of an atom?
What is the maximum number of electrons that can occupy the second electron shell of an atom?
What term describes the electrons found in an atom's outermost shell, which determine how it bonds with other atoms?

at_l1_t3.technicalIntricacy: Electron shells fill up in a specific order with fixed maximum capacities (2, then 8, then 8 again for lighter elements), and the electrons in the outermost, incompletely filled shell — the valence electrons — are the ones primarily responsible for how an atom bonds with others.
at_l1_t3.realPurpose: Understanding shell capacity and valence electrons explains the entire structure of the periodic table and predicts how different elements will chemically react with one another.

variants.question: What term describes atoms of the same element that have the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons?
Do isotopes of the same element have the same atomic number, or different atomic numbers?
Do isotopes of the same element have the same mass number, or different mass numbers?

at_l1_t4.technicalIntricacy: Isotopes share the exact same number of protons (and therefore the same atomic number, since that's what defines the element), but differ in their number of neutrons, which changes their mass number without changing which element they are.
at_l1_t4.realPurpose: Isotopes are important in real applications like radiometric dating of ancient objects, medical imaging, and nuclear power, all of which rely on differences between isotopes of the same element.

variants.question: An atom has {{electronCount}} electrons in total. Using the shell-filling rule (2, then 8, then 8), how many electrons are in its outermost shell?
distractors: {{electronCount}}
{{outermostLess}}
{{outermostMore}}

at_l2_t3.technicalIntricacy: Electrons fill the innermost shell first (up to 2), then the next shell (up to 8), and so on; the outermost shell simply holds whatever electrons remain after the inner shells have been completely filled.
at_l2_t3.realPurpose: The number of electrons in the outermost shell directly determines an element's chemical behaviour and its position within a group on the periodic table.

at_l2_t4.questionTemplate: An atom has a mass number of {{massNumber}} and contains {{neutrons}} neutrons. How many protons does it have?
at_l2_t4.technicalIntricacy: Since mass number equals protons plus neutrons, the number of protons can be found by subtracting the number of neutrons from the mass number — the reverse of finding neutrons from atomic and mass number.
at_l2_t4.realPurpose: Being able to work this relationship in any direction (finding protons, neutrons, or mass number from the other two) is essential for fully understanding an atom's structure from partial information.

variants.question: A student finds that two different atoms both have a mass number of {{massNumber}} and assumes they must be the same element. What is the mistake in this reasoning?
variants.answer: Mass number alone doesn't determine the element — different elements can coincidentally share the same mass number if one has more protons and fewer neutrons while another has fewer protons and more neutrons (called isobars); it is specifically the atomic number (number of protons) that determines which element an atom is, not the mass number
distractors: The student is correct — any two atoms sharing the same mass number must always be the exact same element
Mass number and atomic number are actually two different names for the exact same property
Two atoms can only share the same mass number if they are isotopes of each other, never different elements

at_l3_t3.technicalIntricacy: Mass number is simply the total count of protons and neutrons, and this total can be reached through different combinations — one element might have more protons and fewer neutrons, while a different element reaches the identical total with fewer protons and more neutrons; only the atomic number (proton count alone) uniquely identifies an element.
at_l3_t3.realPurpose: This distinction (atoms called 'isobars') shows why atomic number, not mass number, is used to organise the periodic table and define what makes an element unique.

variants.question: A student believes electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed, perfectly circular orbits, like tiny planets orbiting a sun. What is a more accurate understanding at this level?
variants.answer: Electrons move very rapidly within a shell rather than following one neat fixed circular path; the shell diagram is a simplified model showing how many electrons occupy each energy level, not a literal snapshot of their real-time positions
distractors: The student is correct — electrons follow perfectly fixed, precisely knowable circular orbits at all times, exactly like tiny planets
Electrons don't move at all; they remain completely stationary within their assigned shell
Electrons only follow fixed circular orbits in heavier elements, but move randomly in lighter ones

at_l3_t4.technicalIntricacy: The simple shell diagrams used at this level are a helpful simplification for understanding basic chemical behaviour — they correctly show how many electrons occupy each shell, which is what determines an element's reactivity, even though electrons don't actually stay fixed on a single drawn circle.
at_l3_t4.realPurpose: Understanding that shell diagrams are a useful simplification (rather than a literal picture) is an important lesson in how science uses models to explain behaviour without needing every physical detail to be exact.

variants.question: In a neutral atom (one with no overall electric charge), how does the number of electrons compare to the number of protons?
Why is a neutral atom electrically neutral overall, even though it contains both positively and negatively charged particles?
variants.answer: Because it has exactly as many electrons (negative) as protons (positive), so their charges exactly cancel out

distractorPool: Because it has exactly as many electrons (negative) as protons (positive), so their charges exactly cancel out
There are always more protons than electrons
There are always more electrons than protons
at_l1_t5.technicalIntricacy: Every proton's positive charge is identical in size to every electron's negative charge, so an atom is only electrically neutral when it contains precisely the same number of each; any imbalance between them would leave the atom electrically charged overall.
at_l1_t5.realPurpose: This equal balance is the default state of every atom, and it is precisely what changes when atoms lose or gain electrons to form charged ions.

variants.question: What is the general term for a particle formed when a neutral atom gains or loses one or more electrons?
When a neutral atom loses one or more electrons, does it become a positively charged ion or a negatively charged ion?
When a neutral atom gains one or more electrons, does it become a positively charged ion or a negatively charged ion?

at_l1_t6.technicalIntricacy: Losing electrons removes some of an atom's negative charge, leaving an excess of positive charge (a positive ion), while gaining electrons adds extra negative charge, giving the atom an overall negative charge (a negative ion); either way, the number of protons in the nucleus itself never changes.
at_l1_t6.realPurpose: Ion formation is the basis of ionic bonding, which holds together compounds like common salt (sodium chloride), and underlies how batteries and many biological processes work.

variants.question: Compared to a proton, is the mass of an electron very similar, or very much smaller?
variants.answer: Very much smaller (roughly a couple of thousand times lighter)

variants.question: Which two subatomic particles have approximately equal mass to each other, roughly 1 atomic mass unit each?

distractorPool: Very much smaller (roughly a couple of thousand times lighter)
Very similar in mass to a proton
at_l1_t7.technicalIntricacy: Protons and neutrons have almost identical masses to one another (about 1 atomic mass unit each), while electrons are so much lighter (roughly 1/1800th the mass of a proton) that their contribution to an atom's total mass is considered negligible.
at_l1_t7.realPurpose: This is exactly why mass number only counts protons and neutrons — adding the electrons' mass would barely change the total at all.

variants.question: Compared to the overall size of an atom, is the nucleus relatively large or extremely small?
variants.answer: Extremely small (the nucleus occupies only a tiny fraction of the atom's total volume)

variants.question: Even though it contains almost all of an atom's mass, why is most of an atom's volume actually empty space?
variants.answer: Because the electrons occupy a much larger surrounding region while the tiny, dense nucleus takes up only a very small part of that space

distractorPool: Extremely small (the nucleus occupies only a tiny fraction of the atom's total volume)
Because the electrons occupy a much larger surrounding region while the tiny, dense nucleus takes up only a very small part of that space
Roughly the same size as the atom itself
The atom actually has no empty space inside it at all
at_l1_t8.technicalIntricacy: Almost all of an atom's mass is packed into its extremely small, dense nucleus, while its electrons occupy a much larger surrounding volume, meaning the vast majority of an atom's total volume is actually empty space.
at_l1_t8.realPurpose: This surprising fact (mostly empty space) is one of the key discoveries of early 20th-century physics, and helps explain how certain particles can pass straight through matter with minimal interaction.

variants.question: Electron shells are traditionally labelled with letters starting from the one closest to the nucleus. What is the letter used for the very first (innermost) shell?
What letter is traditionally used to label the second electron shell, just after the innermost (K) shell?

at_l1_t9.technicalIntricacy: Electron shells are traditionally labelled K, L, M, N (and so on) starting from the shell closest to the nucleus, a naming convention that lets chemists refer to a specific shell precisely, alongside the simpler 1st/2nd/3rd shell numbering.
at_l1_t9.realPurpose: These shell labels appear throughout chemistry textbooks and diagrams, so recognising them helps in reading and interpreting electron arrangement diagrams correctly.

variants.question: Since the actual mass of an atom in grams is far too small to be convenient, what unit is commonly used instead to express atomic masses?

at_l1_t10.technicalIntricacy: Atoms are so incredibly small and light that measuring their mass in grams would require extremely tiny, inconvenient numbers, so scientists instead use the atomic mass unit (u), a much more practical scale defined relative to the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
